Enter your balance, rate, months left and any plan fees in the biweekly mortgage calculator below to see the result for your own loan. It returns the months saved, the interest saved and the half-payment, and it also shows the same 13th payment made with no biweekly plan. Take a $300,000 balance at 6.5% with 360 months left. At ModernWallet, we ran that loan three ways in an internal calculation: monthly, biweekly, and monthly with 1/12 of a payment added. The monthly payment is $1,896.20, and biweekly half-payments of $948.10 save $88,121.78 in interest. Adding $158.02 a month instead saves $87,256.29, which is $865.49 less and needs no plan. You can check every figure by changing the inputs in the calculator. The figures above are placeholders. Leave the fees at $0 if you set up biweekly payments yourself. Enter them if a servicer or company charges for a biweekly plan. Biweekly payments end the loan 5 years 10 months sooner $948.10 every two weeks instead of $1,896.20 a month (principal and interest) Interest saved (biweekly) $88,122 Paid off in 24 years 2 months Same 13th payment, no plan $87,256 interest saved Add $158.02 (1/12 of a payment) to each monthly payment and the loan ends in 24 years 2 months, 5 years 10 months sooner, with no fees and no half-payments to time. Monthly schedule 30 years Interest, monthly schedule $382,633 Estimate only. Assumes a fixed-rate loan and principal and interest only (taxes and insurance not included). Biweekly results assume each half-payment is applied the day it is paid. Under Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.36(c) , a servicer may hold a payment smaller than a full monthly payment until a full payment builds up, which would make the biweekly savings somewhat smaller. How it works The biweekly mortgage calculator sets the monthly payment with payment = balance × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where r is the annual rate divided by 12 and n is the months left. A biweekly plan pays half that amount every two weeks. That is 26 half-payments a year, or the value of 13 monthly payments. Each two-week period is charged the annual rate divided by 26 in interest, and each half-payment is applied the day it is paid. On the example loan, the biweekly schedule takes 628 half-payments, about 289.8 months. Total interest falls from $382,633.47 to $294,511.68. The calculator covers fixed-rate loans and shows principal and interest only, so taxes, insurance and escrow are not included. The calculator assumes your servicer applies each half-payment the day it arrives, and a servicer may hold it instead. Regulation Z, at 12 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 1026.36(c)(1), says a servicer must credit a full periodic payment as of the date it is received. A half-payment is a partial payment, so the servicer may hold it in a suspense or unapplied-funds account and show it on the periodic statement. Once enough builds up to cover a full payment, the servicer must treat the funds as a payment received. If your servicer holds half-payments, the real saving is somewhat smaller than the calculator shows, so ask your servicer whether it applies each half-payment on arrival. You can get almost the same result with no plan by adding 1/12 of the monthly payment to each monthly payment. That path also adds 13 payments' worth a year, and it does not depend on when the servicer applies a half-payment. On the example loan, the extra is $158.02 a month. The loan ends in 290 months, 70 months sooner, with $87,256.29 saved in interest. That is $865.49 less than the biweekly saving. Plan fees come out of the interest you save, and the calculator shows the plan fees over the loan and the interest saved after fees. As an illustration, take a $400 setup fee plus $2.50 per debit. Over 628 debits, those fees cost $1,970. That leaves $86,151.78 saved after fees, which is less than the $87,256.29 the free 1/12-extra path saves. A lower rate also shrinks the saving: take the same $300,000 at 3% for 360 months. The payment is $1,264.81, and biweekly saves $20,637.30 in interest. At 0% interest, biweekly saves $0. Skip a paid biweekly plan if your rate is low, if your servicer holds half-payments, or if the fee is larger than the gap between the plan and the 1/12-extra path. If your servicer applies each half-payment the day it arrives and charges no fee, its biweekly option saves $865.49 more than the 1/12-extra path on the example loan. Based on our internal calculation, biweekly payments end the example loan about 70 months sooner, and adding 1/12 of a payment each month comes within $865.49 with no plan. That saving depends on the rate, falling to $20,637.30 at 3% and $0 at 0%. On the example loan, biweekly payments cut total interest from $382,633.47 to $294,511.68, a saving of $88,121.78. At 0% interest, biweekly saves nothing. A plan fee, or a servicer that holds half-payments, lowers the saving. Is a biweekly plan better than paying extra each month? The two give almost the same result. It must show those funds on the periodic statement and treat them as a payment once they cover a full payment. If your servicer holds half-payments, the real saving is somewhat smaller than the calculator shows, so ask the servicer how it applies them. Is a biweekly mortgage plan worth a fee? Choosing between these two paths comes down to comparing your specific loan rate against your tolerance for market risk. Extra principal payments lock in a reduction in future interest costs, but that cash gets tied up directly in home equity. Investing keeps your money more liquid in a brokerage account, though asset prices fluctuate over time. Pay Off the Mortgage Early vs Invest the Extra Money: Side-by-Side Pay Off the Mortgage Early Invest the Extra Money Return you earn Earns a return exactly equal to your mortgage note rate through eliminated interest charges Earns the return generated by your chosen investment portfolio, which has no fixed rate Certainty of that return Completely guaranteed and shielded from the fluctuations of financial markets Uncertain, with returns that can finish higher or lower than your mortgage interest rate Access to the money later Low liquidity, because money put into home equity cannot be drawn without refinancing or selling High liquidity, because securities in a standard taxable brokerage account can be sold as needed Tax angle Reduces total mortgage interest, which only matters on taxes if you itemize on Schedule A Depends on your own tax situation; this page states no rates What has to be true for it to win Your mortgage rate must beat the net after-tax return produced by your investment portfolio Your net investment portfolio return must finish higher than your mortgage interest rate Effect on monthly cash flow Extra payments reduce the cash you keep each month, and money sent in is hard to get back out Contributions also leave your monthly budget, but the money stays in an account that can generally be sold Emotional and risk factors No exposure to market swings; the return equals your mortgage rate Exposed to price swings; returns can finish below your mortgage rate 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? Choose to pay off the mortgage early if your mortgage rate is high, you value a completely guaranteed financial return, and you place personal value on eliminating debt obligations from your life. Choose to invest the extra money if your mortgage rate is low, you have a multi-year horizon that can ride through market volatility, and you want to maintain access to liquid capital in a taxable brokerage account. A split approach is also entirely reasonable: you can send extra principal payments each month while directing surplus cash into investments. This recommendation is not for individuals who lack a liquid emergency fund, have not claimed their full employer retirement match, or carry higher-rate debt elsewhere on their balance sheet. Our verdict would change if your mortgage contract contains an active prepayment penalty, or if your loan interest rate adjusts to a level where the guaranteed savings outpace your realistic portfolio hurdle rate. Run your own mortgage rate through the Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator before deciding. The Return You Earn Each Way The mathematical mechanism of early debt repayment is straightforward. Every extra dollar of principal you pay saves the interest that dollar would have accrued at your loan's rate for the rest of the loan term. Because this savings is baked into your promissory note, the return from extra payments equals your mortgage rate and is not subject to market swings. Investing your spare cash operates on an entirely different mechanism. Investment returns are not guaranteed, and the net performance of a portfolio over your holding period can land lower than your mortgage rate. When you allocate extra cash to financial markets, you accept price fluctuations in exchange for the possibility of outpacing your borrowing cost. There is no contractual floor protecting your capital. If you want to estimate what varied compounding trajectories look like outside of debt reduction, test your monthly contributions with our Investment Growth Calculator to inspect the mechanics of long-term asset accumulation. Because the return on debt paydown is completely fixed while investment results vary, comparing the two paths requires identifying your hurdle rate. If your mortgage rate is high, matching or beating that rate through a portfolio requires taking on substantial volatility with zero guarantee of success. If your loan carries a lower rate, market investments have a lower performance hurdle to clear, yet the risk of principal loss remains real. You must decide whether you prefer a locked-in interest reduction or an open-ended investment outcome that carries downside risk. To see that tradeoff with your own loan and expected return, use the pay off mortgage or invest calculator , which shows the return investing must beat. Liquidity Differences and Accessing Capital Money sent to your lender as extra principal is hard to get back out once the servicer processes the payment. A residential home is not a liquid asset, and equity trapped inside your property walls cannot be spent at a grocery store or used directly to settle unexpected bills. To convert that accumulated home equity back into spendable cash, you must either take out a home equity line, complete a cash-out refinance, or sell the property entirely. If your income drops or you face an unexpected job interruption, a lender may reject an application to borrow against the very equity you worked to build. Investments held in a standard taxable account can generally be sold. Publicly traded securities can generally be sold on any regular business day during market hours. While selling assets during a market downturn can lock in portfolio losses, the capital remains accessible without asking permission from a mortgage underwriter. This structural divide means that choosing whether to pay down mortgage or invest is also a decision about cash flexibility. Funneling every spare dollar into your loan reduces your total liabilities, but it leaves you asset-rich and cash-poor until the balance hits zero. Keeping money in liquid investments preserves your ability to handle large lifestyle emergencies or career changes without needing to liquidate real estate. The Tax Angle and Itemized Deductions The tax consequences of making extra mortgage payments depend entirely on whether you claim the standard deduction or itemize deductions on your federal return. Under the rules outlined in IRS Publication 936 , you can deduct home mortgage interest only if you itemize deductions on Schedule A of Form 1040. If you take the standard deduction, your mortgage interest provides zero federal tax benefit, meaning your effective borrowing cost is identical to the stated note rate on your monthly mortgage statement. For taxpayers who do itemize deductions, federal law caps the amount of mortgage principal eligible for an interest deduction. For debt secured after December 15, 2017, the deduction limit applies to up to $750,000 of acquisition debt, or $375,000 if you are married filing separately. Mortgages originated on or before that date fall under a grandfathered limit covering up to $1 million of acquisition debt. If your loan balance exceeds these statutory caps, only the interest paid on the allowable portion of the debt qualifies for a deduction on Schedule A. When you prepay principal on a mortgage whose interest you actively deduct, your annual interest charges drop, which directly shrinks your itemized tax write-offs. This dynamic reduces the net after-tax savings of your prepayments compared to someone taking the standard deduction. If you want to see how loan terms, total interest costs, and amortization schedules shift under different structural setups, look through our analysis of a 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage to understand the baseline interest charges you are attempting to reduce. What to Fund Before Making Either Choice Directing discretionary cash toward early mortgage payments or brokerage accounts usually comes after you have a baseline financial buffer. A reasonable order to check first begins with assembling a fully funded emergency cash reserve, capturing any available employer retirement matching contributions, and paying down higher-interest debt obligations. Skipping these foundational steps to accelerate mortgage payments can leave your household exposed if a sudden financial shock occurs. For a structured look at tackling personal liabilities systematically, examine our framework on how to Pay Off Debt or Invest across multiple debt categories. If your company provides a matching contribution on retirement accounts, every dollar you contribute up to that threshold yields an instant return before any investment growth occurs. Diverting money away from an employer match to prepay a mortgage means walking away from direct compensation. Higher-interest debt costs more than your mortgage, so people usually pay it first. Before you remit extra money to your loan servicer, you must also check whether your specific loan agreement includes a prepayment penalty clause. A penalty for paying off your mortgage early can count as home mortgage interest according to IRS Publication 936, provided the penalty is not assessed for a specific administrative service. More practically, incurring a direct financial fee from your lender simply for paying off principal early immediately erodes the interest savings you are trying to capture. Cash Flow Realities and Structural Alternatives Extra payments and investing both reduce the cash you keep each month. Investing the extra cash allows you to build an accessible pool of capital that can help cover monthly obligations during leaner periods. If you retain your standard loan amortization schedule and put surplus cash into an investment account, those funds remain available if your household experiences an income interruption. With extra mortgage payments, that liquidity is gone unless you borrow against the equity, refinance, or sell. If your primary motivation is lowering interest costs or reducing your monthly obligation, refinancing to a new term or lower rate might offer an alternative mechanism to evaluate alongside extra payments. You can use our Mortgage Refinance Calculator to review whether adjusting your baseline borrowing terms accomplishes your debt reduction goals without requiring you to manually accelerate monthly payments. Refinancing has its own closing costs, which this page does not quantify, so price them before comparing it with extra payments. Frequently asked questions Should I pay off my mortgage early or invest? Paying off your mortgage early earns a guaranteed return equal to your note rate, while investing offers a return that is not guaranteed and can finish higher or lower. Your decision rests on your loan's interest rate, your tolerance for market risk, and whether you prefer liquid assets in a brokerage account over equity locked inside your home. Is it better to pay extra on a mortgage or invest in the stock market? Neither path is universally better because each serves a different financial objective. Paying extra principal eliminates debt with zero risk of market loss, whereas investing exposes your cash to market downturns in pursuit of portfolio growth. If your mortgage rate is high, extra payments save that higher rate with no market risk, so an investment has more to beat. Does paying off a mortgage early save taxes? Paying off a mortgage early reduces your annual interest expense, which only alters your taxes if you itemize deductions on Schedule A. Under IRS Publication 936, taxpayers who take the standard deduction receive no tax deduction for mortgage interest anyway, meaning paying off the loan simply saves the stated interest rate without changing their tax bill. Can I get a prepayment penalty for paying off my mortgage early? Some loan contracts include a prepayment penalty if you pay off principal ahead of schedule. Under IRS Publication 936, a prepayment penalty can be deductible as home mortgage interest if it is not charged for a specific service, but you should always review your note terms before sending extra payments. What should I do before making extra mortgage payments? Before committing extra cash to your mortgage, confirm you have an adequate emergency fund, capture any available employer match in your retirement account, and pay off any higher-interest debt. mainEntity.name: Should I pay off my mortgage early or invest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Paying off your mortgage early earns a guaranteed return equal to your note rate, while investing offers a return that is not guaranteed and can finish higher or lower. Your decision rests on your loan's interest rate, your tolerance for market risk, and whether you prefer liquid assets in a brokerage account over equity locked inside your home.

mainEntity.name: Is it better to pay extra on a mortgage or invest in the stock market?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither path is universally better because each serves a different financial objective. Paying extra principal eliminates debt with zero risk of market loss, whereas investing exposes your cash to market downturns in pursuit of portfolio growth. If your mortgage rate is high, extra payments save that higher rate with no market risk, so an investment has more to beat.

mainEntity.name: Does paying off a mortgage early save taxes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Paying off a mortgage early reduces your annual interest expense, which only alters your taxes if you itemize deductions on Schedule A. Under IRS Publication 936, taxpayers who take the standard deduction receive no tax deduction for mortgage interest anyway, meaning paying off the loan simply saves the stated interest rate without changing their tax bill.

mainEntity.name: Can I get a prepayment penalty for paying off my mortgage early?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some loan contracts include a prepayment penalty if you pay off principal ahead of schedule. Under IRS Publication 936, a prepayment penalty can be deductible as home mortgage interest if it is not charged for a specific service, but you should always review your note terms before sending extra payments.

mainEntity.name: What should I do before making extra mortgage payments?

acceptedAnswer.text: Before committing extra cash to your mortgage, confirm you have an adequate emergency fund, capture any available employer match in your retirement account, and pay off any higher-interest debt.

At the 10.5-mill statewide average, savings are about $1,035 in 2027 and about $2,085 in 2028 for homes assessed above $250,000. Lower-valued homes save less because the exemption cannot exceed the assessed value of the property. Take a home with an assessed value of $400,000 taxed at 10.5 mills. The non-school property tax bill today is $3,660.18 under the current $51,411 exemption. In 2027, the bill drops to $2,625.00 for a savings of $1,035.18. In 2028, the bill falls to $1,575.00, saving you $2,085.18 each year. Share Interactive — edit any field Assessed value of your homestead $ Your non-school millage (mills, from your TRIM notice) Mills are dollars of tax per $1,000 of taxable value. 10.5 is the statewide average for non-school levies. Use the county, city and district lines on your tax bill, not the school line. Florida resident with homestead on Dec 31, 2026? Yes No Yearly savings once fully phased in (2028) $2,085 $1,035 in 2027 (approved by voters Nov 3, 2026) Non-school bill today $3,660 Bill in 2027 $2,625 Bill in 2028 $1,575 Extra value exempt, 2027 $98,589 Extra value exempt, 2028 $198,589 Estimate only. School taxes are not changed by the amendment and are left out. Based on the current $51,411 non-school exemption (less for homes assessed under $76,411: the first $25,000, plus value from $50,000 to $76,411) versus $150,000 (2027) and $250,000 (2028), as published by Florida TaxWatch . Your county's actual millage and any later local changes decide your real bill. Not tax advice. How it works The calculator works out your non-school property tax bill with this formula: tax bill equals assessed value minus the homestead exemption, multiplied by mills divided by 1,000. One mill equals $1 of tax per $1,000 of taxable value. The baseline calculation uses the current non-school exemption figure of $51,411. Florida voters approved Amendment 3 on November 3, 2026 (about 62% yes on election-night reporting, above the 60% needed), so the exemption increases to $150,000 in 2027 and reaches $250,000 in 2028. Only non-school levies change under this proposal. These non-school taxes fund county services, cities, and special districts. School property taxes make up about 40% of the average tax bill and stay completely unchanged. The savings come directly from shielding more value from non-school taxes. In 2027, the $150,000 exemption frees an extra $98,589 from taxation compared to the current $51,411 baseline. In 2028, the $250,000 exemption protects an extra $198,589. At the 10.5-mill average rate, those extra exemptions produce your annual tax reductions. A home assessed at $100,000 pays a non-school bill of $510.18 today at 10.5 mills. That bill drops to $0.00 in 2027 and stays at $0.00 in 2028. Total savings are $510.18 both years, because the exemption cannot exceed the home's value. A $400,000 home taxed at 15 mills pays $5,228.84 today. That bill drops to $3,750.00 in 2027, saving $1,478.84. In 2028, the bill drops to $2,250.00, saving $2,978.84. State economists estimate a recurring local property tax revenue loss of nearly $12 billion. Local governments may adjust future millage rates in response, which would alter your final bill. The tool does not model annual inflation adjustments starting in 2029, the five-year phase-in for newcomers, or the Save Our Homes cap. This tool is not for renters or owners of vacation and rental homes, who receive no homestead exemption. To see how property taxes factor into your total monthly housing payment, use our mortgage calculator . You can also browse all calculators to model other household expenses. Frequently asked questions Did Florida Amendment 3 pass? Yes, Florida voters approved Amendment 3 on November 3, 2026 with about 62% yes on election-night reporting, above the 60% needed, according to the WUSF/News Service of Florida report ; final certified totals may differ slightly. How much will Florida Amendment 3 save me on property taxes? A home assessed above $250,000 saves about $1,035 in 2027 and about $2,085 in 2028 at the 10.5-mill statewide average. Higher millage rates yield larger dollar savings, while lower-valued homes save less because the exemption cannot exceed the property's assessed value. Enter your assessed value and local non-school millage in the calculator above to see your exact figures. What does Florida Amendment 3 change? Amendment 3 raises the homestead exemption for non-school levies to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It also lowers the annual assessment growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%. Existing Save Our Homes rules and personal exemptions remain unchanged. Does Amendment 3 lower school property taxes? No. The amendment does not apply to school property taxes. School taxes make up about 40% of the average tax bill and stay unchanged under the approved amendment. When would the bigger homestead exemption start? The first expansion takes effect on January 1, 2027, raising the non-school exemption to $150,000. The full $250,000 exemption begins on January 1, 2028. Annual inflation adjustments using the Consumer Price Index begin on January 1, 2029. Why do I save less if my home is worth less than $250,000? Your exemption cannot be larger than the assessed value of your home. A home assessed at $100,000 pays zero non-school taxes once the exemption reaches $100,000. Any exemption value beyond the home's total assessed value produces no additional savings. Who gets the full $250,000 exemption? Permanent Florida residents as of December 31, 2026 receive the full expanded exemptions in 2027 and 2028. Newcomers start with a $50,000 exemption and ramp up to $250,000 after five years. Local governments can shorten that five-year waiting period after 2030. What happens to rental and vacation property under Amendment 3? Non-homestead properties do not receive the larger homestead exemption. Instead, commercial, rental, and vacation properties see their annual assessment growth cap drop from 10% to 5%. That cap limits how quickly an assessed value can increase each year. Where do I find my millage rate? The statewide average non-school rate used in published examples is 10.5 mills. Sum the rates for your county, municipality, and special districts while excluding school districts. For more on the amendment and local rates, see the Florida TaxWatch property-tax resource center . Worked Examples at 3% and 7.5% Should You Pay Off Your Mortgage Early or Invest? Worked Examples at 3% and 7.5% By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated November 4, 2026 Whether you should pay off your mortgage early or invest depends on your mortgage rate compared with the return you can reasonably expect from investing. In two worked examples with a $300,000 balance, the loan at 3% ended further ahead by investing an extra $500 a month at an assumed 5% to 7% return. The new loan at 7.5% ended further ahead by prepaying that same $500, even against a 7% return. At ModernWallet, we ran both examples with the same $500 a month. For the broader order of employer 401(k) match, emergency fund, and high-rate debt, start with our pay off debt or invest guide. Tools for this journey Extra mortgage payment → Early mortgage payoff → Compound interest → The Rate Comparison That Decides Mortgage Payoff or Investing Paying extra on a mortgage earns a guaranteed return equal to the mortgage rate, before taxes, while an investment return is an assumption. If your loan charges 3%, every extra dollar of principal earns 3% with certainty. If your loan charges 7.5%, every extra dollar earns 7.5% with certainty. Compare two numbers: your mortgage rate and the annual return you expect from investing the same money. In the examples that follow, a 3% rate lost to both a 5% and a 7% assumed return. A 7.5% rate beat both. Two groups of readers face this choice with very different rates. Owners who locked in a loan near 3% are one group, and new borrowers paying around 7% to 7.5% are the other. Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) data reported by the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) put the September 2026 average 30-year fixed contract rate at 7.1%. Check today's rate on the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey (PMMS) page before you plug a number into the comparison. Worked Example for a Locked-In Owner at 3% For a locked-in owner at 3%, investing the extra $500 a month ended ahead of prepaying at both a 5% and a 7% assumed return. The example starts with a $300,000 balance at 3% and 25 years (300 months) left, with a required payment of $1,422.63 a month. Paid on schedule, the remaining interest totals $126,790. On the prepay path, adding $500 a month pays the loan off in 199 months, about 16.6 years. Total interest drops to $80,729, a saving of $46,061. After payoff, this path invests the freed-up $1,922.63 a month (the old payment plus the extra $500) for the remaining 101 months, through month 300. On the invest path, you keep the regular payment and invest $500 a month for all 300 months. That puts $150,000 of contributions into the account. Here is where each path stands at month 300: Invest $500 a month from month 1: $297,755 at 5%, $405,036 at 7% Prepay, then invest $1,922.63 a month after payoff: $240,821 at 5%, $263,479 at 7% Invest-first lead: $56,934 at 5% ($297,755 minus $240,821) and $141,557 at 7% ($405,036 minus $263,479) Both paths finish month 300 with the mortgage fully paid, so the gap is the size of the investment account. The invest-first account carries market risk that the prepay path avoids while the loan is open. The $46,061 of interest saved is guaranteed. Worked Example for a New Borrower at 7.5% For a new borrower at 7.5%, prepaying the extra $500 a month ended ahead of investing it at both a 5% and a 7% assumed return. The example is a $300,000 loan at 7.5% over 30 years, with a payment of $2,097.64 a month. Paid on schedule, total interest is $455,152. Adding $500 a month pays the loan off in 206 months, about 17.2 years. Total interest falls to $233,428, a saving of $221,724. The prepay path then invests the freed $2,597.64 a month for the remaining 154 months. The invest path keeps the regular payment and invests $500 a month for all 360 months, which adds up to $180,000 in contributions. At month 360, the totals look like this: Invest $500 a month from month 1: $416,129 at 5%, $609,986 at 7% Prepay, then invest $2,597.64 a month after payoff: $559,292 at 5%, $645,302 at 7% Prepay lead: $143,163 at 5% ($559,292 minus $416,129) and $35,316 at 7% ($645,302 minus $609,986) A guaranteed 7.5% beat an assumed 7%, with no market risk on the extra $500 while the loan was open. New borrowers still choosing a loan type can compare a fixed vs adjustable-rate mortgage before deciding how much to prepay. What the Examples Leave Out The worked examples use level payments and monthly compounding, and they leave out several items that can move your result. They do not include: income taxes on investment gains the mortgage interest deduction investment fees The 5% and 7% returns are assumptions chosen to show a range. They are not forecasts of what any account will earn over 25 or 30 years. The guaranteed-versus-uncertain difference also sits outside the totals. A dollar of interest saved by prepaying is locked in at the loan rate. A projected account balance depends on returns landing close to the assumption for the full period, so give the guarantee extra weight when the two paths end up close. The figures are arithmetic and are not tax advice. Your after-tax result depends on your own tax situation, which the examples do not model, so treat the gaps above as pre-tax gaps. To run the comparison with your own balance, rate, extra amount, return and tax rate, use the pay off mortgage or invest calculator . A Decision Rule to Pay Off Your Mortgage Early or Invest Prepay when your mortgage rate is at or above the return you expect from investing, and invest when the expected return is clearly higher and you can accept market risk. Here is how the two examples line up with that rule: Rate near 3%, expected return of 5% to 7%: investing ended ahead by $56,934 to $141,557 in the locked-in owner example. Rate near 7.5%, expected return of 5% to 7%: prepaying ended ahead by $35,316 to $143,163 in the new borrower example, with no market risk on the extra payments. Rate and expected return close together: the guarantee deserves more weight. Capture any employer 401(k) match, build a starter emergency fund, and handle high-rate debt before applying this rule. Those steps come first in the pay off debt or invest guide. Two changes would flip the verdict. If you expect investments to earn less than 3%, prepaying a 3% loan wins on the same guaranteed-return logic. If you expect returns above 7.5%, the 7.5% case moves toward investing, though that higher return would still be uncertain. Where the Extra Money Should Go First Extra money should go to an employer 401(k) match, a starter emergency fund, and high-rate debt before either extra mortgage payments or investing. That order comes from our pay off debt or invest guide. Once the match is captured, compare a 401(k) vs Roth IRA (individual retirement account) for your retirement dollars. Size your cushion with how much emergency fund you need before you lock extra cash into the loan. If you choose prepayment, check your loan for a prepayment penalty and tell your servicer that extra money should apply to principal, as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) advises on its page about paying extra on a mortgage . More mortgage tools sit on the mortgage hub . Then enter your balance, rate, and extra amount in the extra payment calculator . Run the same monthly amount through the compound interest calculator , and compare both totals before you decide whether to pay off your mortgage early or invest. Frequently asked questions Should I pay off my mortgage early or invest? Compare your mortgage rate to the return you expect from investing. In a $300,000 example, investing $500 a month beat prepaying a 3% loan at both 5% and 7% returns, while prepaying a 7.5% loan beat investing at both. The prepay return is guaranteed, and the investment return is an assumption. Capture any employer 401(k) match and build a starter emergency fund before either choice. Is it better to invest than pay extra on a 3% mortgage? In the worked example, investing came out ahead. Investing $500 a month for 300 months reached $297,755 at 5% and $405,036 at 7%, ahead of the prepay-then-invest path by $56,934 and $141,557. That lead depends on assumed returns, while the $46,061 interest saving from prepaying is guaranteed. Is it worth paying extra on a 7.5% mortgage? Yes, in the worked example. Adding $500 a month to a $300,000 loan at 7.5% saved $221,724 in interest and paid the loan off in about 17.2 years. Prepaying and then investing ended ahead of investing alone by $143,163 at a 5% return and $35,316 at 7%. Does the mortgage interest deduction change the math? Enter an amount in today's dollars, a number of years, and an inflation rate in the calculator above. You can also add an optional annual return if the money is invested. The tool has no historical price data built in. For measured price changes, use the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) . For example, enter $10,000, a 3% inflation rate, and 10 years. The same purchases then cost $13,439. Held unchanged, the $10,000 buys only what $7,441 buys today. That is a 25.6% loss of buying power. Kept as cash, the money has a real return of -2.91% a year. Add a 5% annual return and the real return after inflation becomes 1.94% a year. The balance grows to $16,289, which is worth $12,121 in today's dollars. For the latest 12-month price change, see the BLS Consumer Price Index . Rates below 0% (deflation) are not supported. A minus sign is ignored. Annual return on the money (optional) % The 3% inflation rate above is a placeholder, not a forecast. Enter the rate you want to test. Leave the return at 0 to see money held as cash. Cost later of what $10,000 buys today $13,439 after 10.0 years at 3.0% a year What $10,000 buys then, in today's dollars $7,441 Buying power lost 25.6% Years for buying power to halve 23.4 Real return after inflation -2.91% Ending balance at the return $10,000 That balance in today's dollars $7,441 Estimate only. Assumes one steady inflation rate every year, while real inflation changes from year to year and differs by what you buy. For measured price changes, see the Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI data. Arithmetic, not a forecast or advice. Show year-by-year Further reading on beating inflation The Bogleheads' Guide to Investing by Taylor Larimore, Mel Lindauer and Michael LeBoeuf How to move idle cash into low-cost index funds that can outpace the inflation rate you entered. Check price on Amazon How to Make Your Money Last by Jane Bryant Quinn How to make savings last while prices rise. Check price on Amazon As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases. How it works The calculator takes an amount in today's dollars and raises the price of what it buys by your inflation rate, compounded once a year for the number of years you enter. The formula is future cost = amount x (1 + inflation)^years. Enter $10,000, a 3% rate, and 10 years. The same purchases then cost $13,439 at the end of the period. Buying power uses the same math in reverse. The calculator divides your amount by (1 + inflation)^years to show what it will buy later, measured in today's dollars. With the same inputs, $10,000 held unchanged buys what $7,441 buys today, a 25.6% loss of buying power. The calculator also reports how long buying power takes to halve, using ln 2 / ln(1 + inflation), which comes to about 23.4 years at 3%. Real return is what money earns each year after inflation is taken out, and the calculator computes it as (1 + nominal return) / (1 + inflation) - 1. Held as cash at 0%, the money has a real return of -2.91% a year against 3% inflation. At a 5% annual return, the real return rises to 1.94% a year. The $10,000 then grows to $16,289 in future dollars, which is worth $12,121 in today's dollars. Compare that $12,121 with the $7,441 the same money buys after sitting as cash. The inflation rate is an input because one rate cannot describe every year or every budget. Real inflation changes from year to year, and the prices of different things rise at different speeds. The 3% in the tool is a placeholder for you to replace, so run several rates and watch how far the future cost and real return move. Measured price changes come from the CPI program the BLS publishes, and this calculator does not include that data. The calculator assumes one steady inflation rate in every year of the period. It does not model taxes or fees on the return, so the ending balance and the real return are both shown before those costs. To work out a return figure first, use the compound interest calculator , the high-yield savings calculator , or the CD calculator , then enter that rate here to see what it earns after inflation. Frequently asked questions How do I calculate the effect of inflation on money? Multiply the amount by (1 + inflation rate) raised to the number of years to get the future cost of the same purchases. Divide the amount by that same factor to see what it buys later in today's dollars. For example, enter $10,000 and 3% for 10 years in the calculator above. The future cost is $13,439, and the unchanged amount buys what $7,441 buys today. What is the formula for future cost with inflation? Future cost equals the amount times (1 + inflation) raised to the number of years. In the formula the rate is written as a decimal, so 3% becomes 0.03, while the calculator takes it as a percent. Applied to $10,000 over 10 years, the formula gives $13,439. What inflation rate should I enter? The calculator does not pick a rate for you. The 3% in the tool is a placeholder, and you can test several rates to see how much the future cost and buying power change. For measured price changes, use the Consumer Price Index data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics . What does real return mean? Real return is the yearly growth of your money after inflation is removed. The calculator uses (1 + nominal return) / (1 + inflation) - 1. A 5% return with 3% inflation gives a real return of 1.94% a year. For a second explanation, read the real rate of return entry on Investor.gov , the investor site of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Why does money held as cash lose value? Cash in this calculator earns 0%, so prices rise each year while the balance stays the same. At 3% inflation, cash has a real return of -2.91% a year. Over 10 years, $10,000 held as cash buys what $7,441 buys today. That is 25.6% less buying power. How long does it take for inflation to halve my buying power? At 3% inflation, buying power halves in about 23.4 years. The calculator finds this with ln 2 / ln(1 + inflation). Does this calculator use historical CPI data? No. The calculator has no historical CPI data built in, so you supply the inflation rate yourself. Measured price changes are published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI program . Can I use this for retirement planning? It covers one part of retirement planning. The calculator shows how a fixed amount loses buying power over a retirement-length horizon at the rate you enter, and the optional return shows the ending balance in today's dollars. It does not model taxes, fees, withdrawals, or a rate that changes over time. For a full projection, use the retirement planning pages . Enter your current balance, interest rate, months left and lump sum in the mortgage recast calculator below, along with any recast fee your servicer charges. The calculator returns the new payment, the interest saved and the months a fee takes to earn back, and it also shows the same lump sum prepaid without a recast. For example, take a $238,000 balance at 6.875% with 312 months left. The payment is $1,639.33 a month in principal and interest. A $30,000 recast cuts it to $1,432.69, which is $206.64 a month less. Share Interactive — edit any field Current loan balance $ Interest rate % Months left Lump sum toward principal $ Lender's recast fee $ Copy the balance, rate and months left from your mortgage statement. The figures above are placeholders. Ask your servicer for its recast fee and minimum lump sum; both vary by lender. New payment after the recast $1,432.69 down $206.64 a month from $1,639.33 (principal and interest) New balance $208,000 Interest saved (recast) $34,471 Fee earned back in 2 months Interest saved, after the fee $34,221 Same lump sum, no recast $109,002 interest saved Keep paying $1,639.33 and the loan ends in 19 years, 7 years sooner, with no fee. A recast lowers the payment instead and saves less interest. Estimate only. Assumes a fixed-rate loan, the same rate and months left after the recast, and principal and interest only (taxes and insurance not included). Not every loan can be recast: your servicer decides, and many do not recast government-backed loans such as FHA and VA loans. How it works The mortgage recast calculator sets a payment with payment = balance × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where r is the annual rate divided by 12 and n is the months left. A recast reruns the formula on the lower balance with the same r and n. On the example loan, the new $208,000 balance gives a payment of $1,432.69, down from $1,639.33. Enter the recast fee your servicer charges, and the calculator shows how many months of the lower payment it takes to earn the fee back. On the example, a $250 fee is earned back in 2 months, and the recast still saves $34,221.26 in interest after the fee. Prepay $30,000 without a recast and keep paying $1,639.33, and the lower balance clears the example loan in 228 months. That is 84 months, or 7 years, sooner, with $109,002.12 saved in interest. The recast saves $34,471.26, so it gives up interest savings in exchange for a lower required payment. A recast fits a borrower who wants a lower required payment, for example after a home sale or a drop in income. Enter your balance, rate, term, and extra payment above to see your new payoff date. Even a small extra monthly payment can shave years off a 30-year loan. The calculator does the math, letting you compare scenarios in seconds. $2,212 monthly payment $303,412 total interest $142,994 saved with extra payments Share Interactive — edit any field How much will extra payments save? Enter your mortgage, then add an extra monthly amount to see the savings. Home price $ Down payment $ Interest rate (APR) % Loan term 10 years 15 years 20 years 30 years Extra payment per month (optional) $ Property tax / year $ Home insurance / year $ HOA / month (optional) $ Total monthly payment $2,387 + $300 extra principal, interest, taxes & insurance (PITI) Principal & interest $2,212 Taxes, insurance + PMI $175 Loan amount $350,000 Total interest $303,412 Payoff time 21 years 9 months Total of payments $653,412 Principal Interest With your extra payment: save $142,994 in interest and pay off 8 years 3 months sooner (vs. 30 years on the original schedule) Show amortization schedule (261 payments) Download full schedule (CSV) How it's calculated A mortgage extra payment calculator applies any amount above your scheduled payment directly to your loan principal. Lowering the principal faster means less interest accrues over the life of the loan. That is why a modest monthly extra can save tens of thousands of dollars. The tool first finds your scheduled principal-and-interest payment. It then adds your extra amount each month and rebuilds the payoff schedule. You see your new payoff date, total interest, and lifetime savings side by side with the original loan. A worked example Consider a $350,000 mortgage at 6.5% for 30 years. The scheduled principal-and-interest payment is $2,212.24. With no extra payments, the loan runs the full 360 months and costs about $446,406 in interest. Now add $300 extra every month. In month one, $1,895.83 goes to interest. The scheduled payment puts $316.41 toward principal, and your extra $300 brings the total principal reduction to $616.40. Keeping that $300 going, the loan is paid off in 261 months, about 21 years and 9 months. Total interest drops to $303,412. That is $142,994 saved in interest and 99 months, over eight years, cut from the term. Common mistakes to avoid Not telling your servicer to apply the extra money to principal. The CFPB warns that servicers may otherwise put it toward next month's payment or escrow, so add a written note or use the principal-only option. Paying for a third-party biweekly plan. The CFPB notes you can get the same result for free by sending one extra payment a year yourself, instead of paying a setup or service fee. Skipping a check for a prepayment penalty before you start. These usually apply only in the first three to five years, but confirm with your lender first. Funneling extra cash into the mortgage before higher-rate debt or an emergency fund. Mortgage money is hard to pull back out once it is paid. Confusing your total monthly payment with principal and interest. Taxes and insurance in escrow do not pay down the loan, so base your extra payment on the P&I figure. Frequently asked questions How much do I save with a mortgage extra payment calculator? It depends on your loan, but the savings are large. On a $350,000 loan at 6.5% for 30 years, adding $300 a month saves $142,994 in interest and pays the loan off 99 months early. Enter your own numbers in the calculator above to see your figures. Does one extra mortgage payment a year really help? Yes. One extra payment a year still cuts years off a 30-year loan: about 70 months on a $300,000 loan at 6.5%, and fewer at lower rates. A biweekly schedule does the same thing: paying half your amount every two weeks adds up to 26 half-payments, or 13 full monthly payments, each year. How do I make sure extra payments go to principal? Tell your servicer in writing to apply the extra amount to principal. The CFPB cautions that without instructions, a servicer may apply extra money to the next payment or to escrow instead of reducing your balance. Will I pay a penalty for paying my mortgage early? Usually not for small extra principal payments. The CFPB says prepayment penalties typically apply only if you pay off the whole balance within the first three to five years. Check your loan documents or ask your lender to be sure. Is a biweekly plan better than just paying extra? Both reach the same goal, but doing it yourself is free. Third-party biweekly plans can charge setup or service fees. You can match the result by adding one extra payment a year on your own, or using the calculator above to set a monthly extra amount. To compare the two schedules side by side, use the biweekly mortgage calculator . Should I pay extra on my mortgage or invest the money instead? It depends on your rate. Prepaying a 6.5% mortgage is a guaranteed 6.5% return, while investing that same money is a real edge only if the market beats your rate over your full time horizon, with no guarantee it will. A sub-4% mortgage tips the math toward investing instead. See the full worked comparison, side by side, in our guide on whether to pay off debt or invest . Investments grow monthly at your annual return, and at the end, tax is charged on gains (balance minus contributions) at your tax rate. Both homes are paid off by the original payoff date, so the comparison comes down to the after-tax invested balance on each path. The break-even return is the annual return at which both paths end equal. Compare it with the return you expect after fees. Below the break-even, paying off early wins, and above it, investing wins. That includes attorney fees (statutory in 9 states and reasonable-fee in ~41), executor commission, court filing fees, and any ancillary probate required for out-of-state real property. Where an actual state fee schedule exists, the calculator above applies it. California follows Cal. Prob. Code §10810, with 4%/3%/2%/1%/0.5% tiers. Florida follows Fla. Stat. §733.6171, with a $1,500 base plus tiered percentages. Another 7 states have their own statutes. For a moderate California estate valued at $750,000, the total probate cost runs about $36,000 to $42,000 over 15 to 30 months. By comparison, a revocable living trust that would have avoided probate entirely costs $2,025 to $6,750. Probate calculators Probate Fee Calculator Free · instant Probate Timeline Calculator Free · instant Probate Vs Living Trust Calculator Free · instant How it works Probate cost has four components. First, attorney fees — California, Florida, Iowa, Missouri, Montana, New York (executor only), Wyoming, Arkansas, Oklahoma, and New Jersey (executor only) set statutory schedules; every other state uses a reasonable-fee model at roughly 2-4% of gross estate. Second, executor commission — in California and Iowa, both the attorney and executor get the same statutory percentage, roughly doubling the bill. Third, court filing fees + publication + certified copies, typically $400-$1,500 uncontested, $900-$4,500 contested. Fourth, ancillary probate — a separate probate opened in each additional state where the decedent owned titled real property, running $2,000-$8,000 per additional state. Timelines vary sharply by state. Texas independent administration under Estates Code §401.001 closes in 3-6 months. Uniform Probate Code informal states (Utah, Colorado, Arizona, Minnesota, Idaho) close in 4-8 months. California takes 12-24 months because Prob. Code §9100's 4-month creditor claim period plus urban court backlogs push things out. New York Surrogate's Court runs 12-24 months for anything beyond voluntary administration (SCPA Article 13, available for personal property under $50,000). Contested probate — will contests, creditor litigation — runs 2-5 years everywhere. Every state has a small-estate procedure that lets estates under a threshold skip full probate: California $208,850 (indexed 2025), Texas $75,000 excluding homestead, New York $50,000 personal property (SCPA Article 13), Florida $75,000 or death 2+ years old (summary administration), Wyoming $200,000. The calculator above flags when your estate qualifies. Below the threshold, fees drop to under $1,000 and timeline shortens to weeks. The biggest single lever to reduce probate cost is a revocable living trust set up during life. Because trust assets don't pass through probate, the entire attorney-executor-court stack disappears. The living trust cost calculator shows attorney fees of $1,500-$5,000 for a revocable trust in most states, $5,000-$10,000+ in California and other HNW metros. For any California estate over about $200,000 gross, the trust math wins decisively — a lesson probate teaches families the expensive way. Frequently asked questions What is a probate calculator? A probate calculator estimates the total cost and timeline of probating an estate in your state. Inputs: state, gross estate value, complexity (uncontested vs contested), and number of additional states where real property is located (which triggers ancillary probate). The calculator above applies actual state fee schedules — California's Cal. Prob. Code §10810, Florida's Fla. Stat. §733.6171, and 7 other statutory states — and market-typical percentages for the ~41 reasonable-fee states. How much does probate cost? Probate cost runs 3-8% of gross estate in most states for uncontested cases, or roughly $10,000-$60,000 for typical estates. In statutory-fee states like California, both the attorney and executor get the same percentage schedule (Cal. Prob. Code §10810), so total statutory fees roughly double: a $500,000 California estate faces about $26,000 in combined attorney + executor fees. Reasonable-fee states like Texas and Colorado run 2-4% of gross estate. Contested cases hit $50,000+ almost everywhere. Ancillary probate for real property in additional states adds $2,000-$8,000 per state. How long does probate take? Uncontested probate takes 6-12 months in most states, 9-18 months with real estate, and 12-24 months in California and New York. Texas independent administration closes fastest (3-6 months). Uniform Probate Code informal states (Utah, Colorado, Arizona, Minnesota, Idaho) close in 4-8 months. California is slow because Prob. Code §9100 sets a 4-month creditor claim period plus urban courts run backlogs. Contested probate — will contests or creditor litigation — takes 2-5 years everywhere. Small-estate procedures bypass full probate and close in weeks. Which states have statutory probate fees? Nine states set statutory attorney or executor fee schedules: California (Cal. Prob. Code §10810), Florida (Fla. Stat. §733.6171 attorney + §733.617 PR), Iowa (Iowa Code §633.197/198), Missouri (§473.153), Montana (§72-3-631), New York (SCPA §2307 executor only), Wyoming (§2-7-803), Arkansas (§28-48-108), Oklahoma (tit. 58 §527), and New Jersey (§3B:18-14, executor only). The other ~41 states use a 'reasonable fee' standard subject to court approval on contested cases and market-typical practice on uncontested cases (2-4% of gross estate typical). How can I avoid probate? The most reliable way is a revocable living trust set up during life. Assets titled to the trust pass to beneficiaries at death without going through probate court. Other probate-avoidance tools: transfer-on-death deeds for real estate (available in ~30 states); pay-on-death designations on bank accounts; joint tenancy with rights of survivorship on real estate and vehicles; beneficiary designations on 401(k), IRA, and life insurance (these override wills and trusts). A living trust is the most comprehensive because it covers assets these individual tools miss. See the living trust cost calculator for setup costs by state. What is ancillary probate? Ancillary probate is a separate probate proceeding opened in each state (other than the decedent's domicile) where the decedent owned titled real property — real estate, mineral interests, sometimes vehicles/boats. The domicile-state probate must be opened first; the ancillary state then admits the domicile-state letters testamentary. Cost typically $2,000-$8,000 per additional state, plus 6-12 months of additional timeline. A revocable living trust that holds all real property avoids ancillary probate entirely because the trust doesn't die when the grantor does. How much does probate cost in Michigan, Missouri, Connecticut, South Dakota, or Virginia? It varies widely because these five states don't all use the same fee model. Missouri sets a statutory attorney/executor percentage schedule (Mo. Rev. Stat. §473.153). Michigan and South Dakota use 'reasonable compensation' standards — Michigan with no percentage guideline at all, South Dakota with a non-binding one. Connecticut's statutory fee is actually a probate COURT fee (not an attorney or executor commission), capped at $40,000. Virginia has no attorney/executor fee statute but does levy a separate probate tax on the estate. mainEntity.name: What is a probate calculator?

acceptedAnswer.text: A probate calculator estimates the total cost and timeline of probating an estate in your state. Inputs: state, gross estate value, complexity (uncontested vs contested), and number of additional states where real property is located (which triggers ancillary probate). The calculator above applies actual state fee schedules — California's Cal. Prob. Code §10810, Florida's Fla. Stat. §733.6171, and 7 other statutory states — and market-typical percentages for the ~41 reasonable-fee states.

mainEntity.name: How much does probate cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Probate cost runs 3-8% of gross estate in most states for uncontested cases, or roughly $10,000-$60,000 for typical estates. In statutory-fee states like California, both the attorney and executor get the same percentage schedule (Cal. Prob. Code §10810), so total statutory fees roughly double: a $500,000 California estate faces about $26,000 in combined attorney + executor fees. Reasonable-fee states like Texas and Colorado run 2-4% of gross estate. Contested cases hit $50,000+ almost everywhere. Ancillary probate for real property in additional states adds $2,000-$8,000 per state.

mainEntity.name: How long does probate take?

acceptedAnswer.text: Uncontested probate takes 6-12 months in most states, 9-18 months with real estate, and 12-24 months in California and New York. Texas independent administration closes fastest (3-6 months). Uniform Probate Code informal states (Utah, Colorado, Arizona, Minnesota, Idaho) close in 4-8 months. California is slow because Prob. Code §9100 sets a 4-month creditor claim period plus urban courts run backlogs. Contested probate — will contests or creditor litigation — takes 2-5 years everywhere. Small-estate procedures bypass full probate and close in weeks.

mainEntity.name: Which states have statutory probate fees?

acceptedAnswer.text: Nine states set statutory attorney or executor fee schedules: California (Cal. Prob. Code §10810), Florida (Fla. Stat. §733.6171 attorney + §733.617 PR), Iowa (Iowa Code §633.197/198), Missouri (§473.153), Montana (§72-3-631), New York (SCPA §2307 executor only), Wyoming (§2-7-803), Arkansas (§28-48-108), Oklahoma (tit. 58 §527), and New Jersey (§3B:18-14, executor only). The other ~41 states use a 'reasonable fee' standard subject to court approval on contested cases and market-typical practice on uncontested cases (2-4% of gross estate typical).

mainEntity.name: How can I avoid probate?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most reliable way is a revocable living trust set up during life. Assets titled to the trust pass to beneficiaries at death without going through probate court. Other probate-avoidance tools: transfer-on-death deeds for real estate (available in ~30 states); pay-on-death designations on bank accounts; joint tenancy with rights of survivorship on real estate and vehicles; beneficiary designations on 401(k), IRA, and life insurance (these override wills and trusts). A living trust is the most comprehensive because it covers assets these individual tools miss. See the living trust cost calculator for setup costs by state.

mainEntity.name: What is ancillary probate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ancillary probate is a separate probate proceeding opened in each state (other than the decedent's domicile) where the decedent owned titled real property — real estate, mineral interests, sometimes vehicles/boats. The domicile-state probate must be opened first; the ancillary state then admits the domicile-state letters testamentary. Cost typically $2,000-$8,000 per additional state, plus 6-12 months of additional timeline. A revocable living trust that holds all real property avoids ancillary probate entirely because the trust doesn't die when the grantor does.

mainEntity.name: How much does probate cost in Michigan, Missouri, Connecticut, South Dakota, or Virginia?

acceptedAnswer.text: It varies widely because these five states don't all use the same fee model. Missouri sets a statutory attorney/executor percentage schedule (Mo. Rev. Stat. §473.153). Michigan and South Dakota use 'reasonable compensation' standards — Michigan with no percentage guideline at all, South Dakota with a non-binding one. Connecticut's statutory fee is actually a probate COURT fee (not an attorney or executor commission), capped at $40,000. Virginia has no attorney/executor fee statute but does levy a separate probate tax on the estate. See the probate fee calculator for the worked numbers and statute citations for each of these five states.

Self-Employment Tax calculators 1099 Tax Calculator Free · instant How Much Should I Set Aside For Taxes 1099 Free · instant DoorDash Taxes Free · instant Uber Driver Taxes Free · instant Uber Eats Taxes Free · instant Lyft Driver Taxes Free · instant Instacart Taxes Free · instant Amazon Flex Taxes Free · instant Shipt Taxes Free · instant Rover Taxes Free · instant Twitch Taxes Free · instant Upwork Taxes Free · instant Fiverr Taxes Free · instant Etsy Seller Taxes Free · instant DataAnnotation Taxes Free · instant YouTube Taxes Free · instant Quarterly Estimated Tax Calculator Free · instant How it works Self-employment tax replaces the Social Security and Medicare taxes an employer would otherwise split with you. A W-2 employee pays 7.65% and the employer pays the matching 7.65%. When you work for yourself you are both parties, so you pay the full 15.3%. The rate is not applied to your full profit. Schedule SE first multiplies net profit by 92.35%, which approximates the employer half an employee would never have been taxed on. That step is why the effective rate on profit is 14.13%, not 15.3% — and why a calculator that skips it overstates your bill by about 8%. The two halves behave differently above a threshold. The 12.4% Social Security portion stops once your combined wages and net earnings reach the wage base, which is $184,500 for 2026. The 2.9% Medicare portion never stops, and an extra 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies above $200,000 ($250,000 for joint filers). If you also hold a W-2 job, those wages consume the Social Security wage base first, so a moonlighter with a high salary can owe far less Social Security tax on their side income than the raw 15.3% suggests. One deduction comes back to you automatically: half of your self-employment tax is an above-the-line deduction against income tax. The calculator applies it, and it excludes the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax, which is not deductible. The set-aside share shown above is deliberately not your household tax bill divided by your profit. If you have a day job, your W-2 withholding already covers the tax on that salary. What you have to fund yourself is the extra tax your self-employment income causes on top of it. That number is often higher than freelancers expect: a side hustle stacks on top of your salary, so it is taxed at your top marginal rate from the first dollar. Someone earning $80,000 at a job plus $20,000 on the side sets aside about 30.5% of the side income, while a full-time freelancer earning $45,000 sets aside about 19.1%. You pay this as you go, not in April. The IRS expects quarterly estimated payments via Form 1040-ES, and there is a penalty for underpaying even if you settle up in full at filing. Our guide to budgeting with irregular income covers the four due dates and the safe-harbor rules that make the penalty go away. Frequently asked questions How much is self-employment tax in 2026? Self-employment tax is 15.3% of net earnings: 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare. Because it applies to 92.35% of your net profit rather than all of it, the effective rate on profit is 14.13%. The Social Security portion stops at $184,500 of combined wages and net earnings in 2026; the Medicare portion has no ceiling, and an extra 0.9% applies above $200,000 ($250,000 married filing jointly). How much should I set aside for taxes as a 1099 contractor? For a full-time freelancer with no other income, 20% to 25% of net profit covers federal self-employment and income tax at typical earnings — $60,000 of profit produces about 20.1%. Set aside more if you have a W-2 job, because side income stacks on top of your salary and is taxed at your highest marginal rate: someone earning $80,000 at a job plus $20,000 freelancing needs about 30.5% of the freelance income. Add your state income tax rate on top of any of these figures. Why is self-employment tax calculated on 92.35% of my profit? Because a W-2 employee is never taxed on the employer's half of FICA, and Schedule SE approximates that treatment for the self-employed. Multiplying net profit by 92.35% removes roughly the employer-share equivalent before the 15.3% rate is applied. It is the reason your real rate is 14.13% of profit, and it happens automatically on Schedule SE — you do not have to elect it. Do I pay self-employment tax if I already pay Social Security at my job? You still pay the 2.9% Medicare portion, but your W-2 wages consume the Social Security wage base first. If your wages already reach $184,500 in 2026, no Social Security tax applies to your self-employment income at all — only Medicare. Below that, the 12.4% applies just to the remaining room under the wage base. Enter your W-2 wages in the calculator above and the breakdown shows exactly how much Social Security tax is left to pay. Do I owe self-employment tax if I made less than $2,000? Self-employment tax applies once your net earnings from self-employment reach $400 for the year — that threshold is unrelated to whether anyone sends you a tax form. For 2026 a payer only has to issue a Form 1099-NEC at $2,000 (raised from $600), and payment apps only issue a 1099-K above $20,000 and 200 transactions. The IRS is explicit that you report gig income "even if the income is... not reported on an information return form." No form does not mean no tax. Can I lower my self-employment tax? Only by lowering net profit, since the tax is charged on profit rather than revenue. Every legitimate business deduction — mileage, home office, software, equipment, supplies — cuts self-employment tax and income tax at the same time, which is why a deduction is worth far more to a 1099 earner than to an employee. Retirement contributions to a SEP-IRA or solo 401(k) reduce income tax but not self-employment tax. At higher profit levels, electing S-corporation treatment can reduce the base the 15.3% applies to, at the cost of running payroll. For 2026 a payer only has to issue a Form 1099-NEC at $2,000 (raised from $600), and payment apps only issue a 1099-K above $20,000 and 200 transactions. The IRS is explicit that you report gig income "even if the income is... not reported on an information return form." No form does not mean no tax.

mainEntity.name: Can I lower my self-employment tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only by lowering net profit, since the tax is charged on profit rather than revenue. Every legitimate business deduction — mileage, home office, software, equipment, supplies — cuts self-employment tax and income tax at the same time, which is why a deduction is worth far more to a 1099 earner than to an employee. Retirement contributions to a SEP-IRA or solo 401(k) reduce income tax but not self-employment tax. At higher profit levels, electing S-corporation treatment can reduce the base the 15.3% applies to, at the cost of running payroll.

It is your net profit: everything you invoiced, minus every legitimate business expense. That figure goes on Schedule C, and it is the number both taxes are calculated from. Self-employment tax comes first. It is 15.3% — 12.4% Social Security plus 2.9% Medicare — applied to 92.35% of net profit rather than all of it, which makes the real rate 14.13% of profit. It is the tax that surprises people, because a W-2 employee only ever sees half of it on their payslip. The Social Security half stops once your combined wages and net earnings reach $184,500 in 2026; the Medicare half never stops. Federal income tax comes second, and it is calculated on a smaller number. Half your self-employment tax is deducted above the line, then the standard deduction ($16,100 single for 2026) comes off, then the 20% qualified business income deduction if you qualify. Only what is left runs through the ordinary brackets. That stacking is why the effective rate is lower than most people fear at modest income, and why the advice to "set aside 30%" is wrong in both directions. On $50,000 of profit the true figure is about 19.5%. Below roughly $17,400 of profit for a single filer with no other income, the standard deduction absorbs everything and federal income tax is zero — leaving only the 14.1% self-employment tax. But the same advice fails the other way for anyone with a job. Freelance income stacks on top of your salary, so it is taxed at your top marginal rate from the very first dollar, while your W-2 withholding already covers the salary. Someone earning $80,000 at a job plus $20,000 freelancing needs to set aside 30.5% of the freelance money, not 19.5%. Enter your W-2 wages above and the tool computes the tax your freelance income actually causes rather than dividing your household bill by your side income. None of this is withheld for you, so you pay it in four instalments through the year using Form 1040-ES. Our guide to budgeting with irregular income covers the due dates and the safe-harbour rule that switches off the underpayment penalty, and the self-employment tax calculator explains the Schedule SE math in full. A worked example Take a freelance designer with $58,000 of invoices and $8,000 of business expenses — software, a laptop, insurance, and an accountant. Net profit is $50,000. Self-employment tax applies to 92.35% of that, or $46,175: 12.4% Social Security is $5,725.70 and 2.9% Medicare is $1,339.08, for $7,064.78 total. Half of that, $3,532.39, is deducted above the line, bringing income down to $46,467.61. The $16,100 standard deduction and a $6,073.52 QBI deduction come off, leaving $24,294.09 of taxable income — $2,667.29 of federal income tax at the 10% and 12% rates. Total federal tax is $9,732.07, which is 19.5% of profit and $2,433.02 due each quarter. Common mistakes to avoid Calculating tax on gross receipts instead of profit. You are taxed on what is left after business expenses, and for many contractors that gap is thousands of dollars. Using a flat 30% set-aside for everything. At $50,000 of profit with no other income the real figure is about 19.5%; with a $80,000 day job on top of $20,000 of freelance income it is 30.5%. One rule of thumb cannot cover both. Forgetting the deduction for half of self-employment tax. It is automatic and above the line, and it lowers the income the brackets apply to. Skipping the 20% QBI deduction. Most Schedule C filers below the §199A threshold qualify, and it is one of the largest deductions available to a contractor. Ignoring state income tax. Every figure here is federal only. Depending on where you live, add anywhere from nothing to more than 10%. Assuming a client who sends no 1099 has reported nothing. The 2026 filing threshold is $2,000 for a 1099-NEC, but your obligation to report starts at $400 of net earnings regardless. Frequently asked questions How much tax do I pay on 1099 income? Self-employment tax of 15.3% on 92.35% of your net profit (an effective 14.13%), plus federal income tax on what remains after the deduction for half your self-employment tax, the standard deduction, and the QBI deduction. On $50,000 of net profit a single filer pays about $9,732 — roughly 19.5% of profit. The percentage rises with income and rises sharply if you also have W-2 wages, because freelance income is taxed on top of your salary. How much should I set aside from each 1099 payment? Between 20% and 25% of profit for a full-time freelancer with no other income, and closer to 30% to 35% if you have a day job, because side income stacks at your top marginal rate. Add your state's income tax rate on top. The most reliable approach is to move the percentage the calculator gives you into a separate savings account the day each payment clears, rather than trying to find the money in April. Do I have to file if I made less than $2,000 and got no 1099? Yes, if your net earnings from self-employment were $400 or more — that threshold, not the 1099 threshold, is what triggers the self-employment tax filing requirement. The $2,000 figure for 2026 is only the point at which the payer must file a Form 1099-NEC, and it went up from $600 this year. The IRS states plainly that gig income is reportable even when no information return is issued. What expenses can I deduct from 1099 income? Anything ordinary and necessary for the work: business mileage, a home office that is used regularly and exclusively for business, software subscriptions, equipment, professional insurance, accounting fees, business phone and internet at the business-use percentage, training, and supplies. Each deduction cuts self-employment tax and income tax at the same time, so for someone in the 12% bracket a deductible dollar is worth about 26 cents rather than 12. When are quarterly taxes due for 1099 income? Estimated payments are generally due four times a year — in April, June, and September, and in January of the following year. Paying at least 90% of the current year's tax, or 100% of last year's (110% if your prior-year AGI was over $150,000), switches off the underpayment penalty even if you end up owing more at filing. That safe harbour is the practical target for anyone whose income varies month to month. Is a 1099 tax calculator accurate enough to pay from? It is accurate enough to set aside from, which is its job. This one uses the real 2026 statutory figures and the actual Schedule SE method rather than a flat percentage, so the quarterly number is a sound basis for estimated payments. It does not model state or local tax, health-insurance or retirement deductions, or credits — all of which move the final figure — so treat the annual return, not the calculator, as the settlement. The advice flips completely if you also have a job. Dashing on top of a salary is taxed at your top marginal rate from the first dollar, because your W-2 withholding already covers the salary.
